limits: No experiments or benchmarks: reflection and multi-agent claims are unquantified assertions.

Supervisor listing is incomplete: researcher and coder are stubs (model.invoke(...)); the Python AgentState declares only next while nodes return messages, and the conditional edge returns state['next'] without mapping FINISH to END (the JS version maps it).
Authors caution these extensions 'shouldn't be the first thing you reach for'; start with the Chapter 6 agent.
Reflection increases latency when appended to an agent.
practices: Use reflection as a generate/reflect loop, inverting message roles in the reflect node so the critic thinks it grades a user's essay (Reflection).
Ground the critique with external information where possible, e.g. run code through a linter or compiler before reflect; 'we strongly recommend giving it a try' (TIP, Reflection).
Terminate after generate in a fixed-iteration loop so the last revisions are applied (Reflection).
Optionally let the reflect step decide when to finish (Reflection).
Attach a subgraph directly as a node when parent and subgraph share state keys; use a wrapper function when schemas differ (Subgraphs).
Give subagents self-explanatory, distinct names, or add descriptions to the supervisor prompt (NOTE, Supervisor Architecture).
Start with the Chapter 6 agent; do not reach first for reflection or multi-agent (Summary).

terms.definition: the creation of a loop between a creator prompt and a reviser prompt
Each agent can communicate with every other agent. Any agent can decide which other agent is to be executed next.

Each agent communicates with a single agent, called the supervisor, which decides which agent (or agents) should be called next. A special case implements the supervisor agent as an LLM call with tools, as covered in Chapter 6.
a multi-agent system with a supervisor of supervisors
Each agent communicates with only a subset of agents. Parts of the flow are deterministic, and only select agents can decide which other agents to call next.
